        # BASE

        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Koch curves start with a simple segment.",
            "We replace parts to increase structural complexity.",
            "Calculating D gives us approximately 1.26.",
            "This fractional value indicates space-filling behavior.",
            "It is more complex than a standard line."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Case Study: The Koch Curve", lecture_lines)
        
        # Define Koch curve iteration
        def get_koch_segment(start, end):
            # Midpoint/triangulation logic
            v = end - start
            p1 = start + v / 3
            p3 = start + 2 * v / 3
            # Rotate for the triangle point
            rot = rotation_matrix(PI / 3, OUT)
            p2 = p1 + np.dot(rot, (v / 3))
            return [start, p1, p2, p3, end]

        def draw_koch(pts, depth):
            if depth == 0:
                return Line(pts[0], pts[-1], color="#F1C40F")
            
            lines = VGroup()
            for i in range(len(pts) - 1):
                new_pts = get_koch_segment(pts[i], pts[i+1])
                lines.add(draw_koch(new_pts, depth - 1))
            return lines

        # Init Line
        start_pt = np.array([-1.5, 0, 0])
        end_pt = np.array([1.5, 0, 0])
        initial_line = Line(start_pt, end_pt, color="#F1C40F")
        self.place_in_area(initial_line, 'B2', 'E5', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#F1C40F")
        self.play(Create(initial_line))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#E67E22")
        koch_1 = draw_koch([start_pt, end_pt], 1)
        self.place_in_area(koch_1, 'B2', 'E5', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(initial_line, koch_1))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#3498DB")
        koch_2 = draw_koch([start_pt, end_pt], 2)
        self.place_in_area(koch_2, 'B2', 'E5', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(koch_1, koch_2))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#2ECC71")
        koch_3 = draw_koch([start_pt, end_pt], 3)
        self.place_in_area(koch_3, 'B2', 'E5', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(koch_2, koch_3))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#9B59B6")
        self.play(koch_3.animate.set_color("#9B59B6"))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Fractal Dimension: Measuring the Complexity of Shapes

sections.title: Introduction: Beyond Integer Dimensions
sections.content: Briefly review Euclidean dimensions (0D point, 1D line, 2D plane, 3D cube). Introduce the intuition that 'length' or 'area' depends on the scale of measurement. Transition to the problem: How do we measure the 'roughness' of shapes that fill space in an unconventional way?
sections.example: Visualizing a line folded repeatedly until it begins to fill a square, hinting at a dimension between 1 and 2.

sections.title: The Self-Similarity Concept
sections.content: Define self-similarity: the property where a part resembles the whole. Establish the scaling relation: N = s^D, where N is the number of new parts, s is the scaling factor, and D is the fractal dimension. Rearrange to find D = log(N) / log(s).
sections.example: An animation showing a Koch Snowflake being constructed; zooming into a segment reveals a shape identical to the whole.

sections.title: Case Study: The Koch Curve
sections.content: Apply the formula to the Koch curve. Step 1: Start with a line segment (s=3). Step 2: Replace with 4 segments (N=4). Step 3: Calculate D = log(4) / log(3) ≈ 1.26. Explain that this fractional value represents its complexity.
sections.example: A side-by-side animation: a straight line 'growing' into a jagged Koch curve, visually demonstrating how 1.26 dimension represents a shape 'thicker' than a line but 'thinner' than a plane.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content: Explain how fractal dimension is used to quantify natural phenomena. High fractal dimensions indicate high complexity and space-filling properties.
sections.example: Comparing the fractal dimension of a blood vessel network (high D, efficient oxygen delivery) versus a simple river tributary system (lower D).

sections.title: Conclusion and Summary
sections.content: Recap the core formula (D = log(N) / log(s)) and the takeaway: Fractal dimension is a measure of how 'densely' a pattern occupies space as we scale down to microscopic detail.
sections.example: Final infographic: A summary card showing the Sierpinski Triangle (D≈1.58) and the Koch Snowflake (D≈1.26) side-by-side to reinforce the scale of complexity.
